title: Why a MILP has no duals

blocks.text: 9.2.1 Why a MILP Has No Duals

GridCap's finance partner asks the question every capital plan meets: "What is one more $1k of capital budget worth?" In lesson 2.3.4 the answer was a shadow price, read from the LP's dual values. GridCap's real plan is the selection model of lesson 1.1.3, where each project is funded or not. That model is a MILP (a mixed-integer linear program: a linear program in which some variables must take whole values). This lesson asks the solver for the MILP's dual values, sees why there are none, and finds out what a dual of a MILP has to be instead. GridCap is a fictional utility; none of its numbers describe a real one.
The Model
The one-period selection model on GridCap's small portfolio (40 projects), with the budget $`B`$ as a parameter, so that later sections can change it.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, each with a parent $`p(c)`$; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups, each a set of projects.
**Parameters.** $`v_i`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ if it starts as early as it can ($k); $`c_i`$, its capital cost ($k); $`B`$, the capital budget ($k; the small portfolio's is 38,390).
**Variables.** $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$: project $`i`$ is funded.
**Objective.**
V(B) \;=\; \max \; \sum_{i \in P} v_i\, x_i
**Constraints.**

The **LP relaxation** (lesson 3.1.1) is the same model with $`0 \le x_i \le 1`$ in place of $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$: a project may be funded in part. The code builds both from one function, `build(portfolio, budget, integer=...)` in `selection.py`, and names each row as the labels do (`budget`, `must_P003`, `parent_P016`, `alt_G001`).
$`V(B)`$, the best NPV the model can reach with budget $`B`$, is the model's **value function**. Read as a function of $`B`$, it is the curve finance is asking about.
A Solver Reports No Dual Values for a MILP
Solve the selection model at the small portfolio's budget and ask for the budget row's dual value, exactly as lesson 2.3.3 did for an LP:

milp = build(small, B)
result = solve_highs(milp.model)
print(f"MILP {result.termination.reason.name}  value {result.objective_value():,.0f}  budget {B:,}")
print("has_dual_feasible_solution:", result.has_dual_feasible_solution())
try:
    result.dual_values(milp.budget)
except ValueError as error:
    print("dual_values:", error)

MILP OPTIMAL  value 25,336  budget 38,390
has_dual_feasible_solution: False
dual_values: Best solution does not have an associated dual feasible solution.

The solve is optimal, and the result says it carries no dual solution. MathOpt's `SolveResult.dual_values` raises `ValueError` in that case, as its docstring says, so a report that reads prices should check `has_dual_feasible_solution()` first, the guard the OR-Tools sample `advanced_linear_programming.py` uses. Lesson 4.2.2 reads the same flag, and lesson 5.3.2 shows gurobipy refusing `Pi` on a MIP in the same way.
This is not a missing feature. The rest of this lesson shows that a MILP has no dual made of one number per row, so the solver has none to give.
The LP Relaxation Has a Price, but It Prices a Plan Nobody Can Fund
The LP relaxation does have dual values. Solve it with GLOP (OR-Tools' simplex solver, lesson 2.4.1):

lp = build(small, B, integer=False)          # the LP relaxation: 0 <= x_i <= 1
relaxed = solve_glop(lp.model)
price = relaxed.dual_values(lp.budget)
print(f"LP relaxation  value {relaxed.objective_value():,.1f}  budget price {clean(price)}")
print(f"gap between the two: {relaxed.objective_value() - result.objective_value():,.1f}")

The relaxation says one more $1k of budget is worth $0.5867k. But its optimum funds 52.2% of project P022, a transmission line that is either built or not. Its value, 25,451.3, is $115.3k above the best plan GridCap can actually fund.

The sign follows MathOpt's convention for a $`\le`$ row in a maximization: the dual value is zero or positive, and it is the rate at which the best value rises as the row's right-hand side grows. Solving the same relaxation with $1k more budget shows the rise directly:
more = solve_glop(build(small, B + 1, integer=False).model)  # the same relaxation with $1k more budget
LP relaxation at B + 1: value 25,451.8533, up 0.5867
So a positive `dual_values` entry on the budget row means more budget, more value: here $0.5867k per $1k, exactly the printed price.

Lesson 2.3.2 proved weak duality for an LP: any feasible dual prices give an upper bound on every plan. The relaxation's prices are feasible prices for the relaxation, and every integer plan is also a plan of the relaxation, so they still bound the MILP: no funded plan is worth more than 25,451.3. What fails is strong duality. For an LP the best bound equals the best plan; here the best bound the LP's prices can give is 25,451.3, and the best plan is 25,336. The difference is the **integrality gap** of lesson 3.1.2. A price whose bound is not tight does not describe the optimum it sits next to, so it is not the MILP's marginal value.
A Price Is a Line That Touches the Value Function From Above, and a Step Function Has Almost None

What does a shadow price mean as a picture? In lesson 2.3.3 the price held over a range: within it, the LP's value moved by exactly price × change. So the line through $`(B, V(B))`$ with slope $`p`$ touched the value curve at $`B`$, and outside the range the curve fell below that line. For an LP this always works, because an LP's value function, for a maximization, is **concave**: the curve never dips below the straight segment (the chord) between two of its points, so at every budget some line touches it from above. In symbols, $`p`$ is a price at $`B`$ when
V(B') \;\le\; V(B) + p\,(B' - B) \qquad \text{for every budget } B'.
The MILP's value function is not concave. Three solves are enough to see it:

values = {b: round(solve_highs(build(small, b).model).objective_value()) for b in (38370, 38380, 38390)}
chord = (values[38370] + values[38390]) / 2
$`V`$ stays at 25,317 from 38,370 to 38,380 and jumps to 25,336 at 38,390. At 38,380 the curve sits below the chord from its neighbours, which a concave function never does.

To see which budgets do get a price, take a model small enough to compute its whole value function. GridCap buys pole-replacement work in three standard packages (this lesson's own example): a package of 3 crew-weeks worth $40k, one of 5 crew-weeks worth $70k, and one of 7 crew-weeks worth $100k. Any whole number of each may be bought, within $`d`$ crew-weeks.

**Sets.** $`J = \{1, 2, 3\}`$, the package types. **Parameters.** $`a_j`$, the crew-weeks package $`j`$ uses, $`a = (3, 5, 7)`$; $`c_j`$, its value in $10k, $`c = (4, 7, 10)`$; $`d`$, the crew-weeks available. **Variables.** $`x_j \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}`$, the number of packages of type $`j`$ bought.

z(d) \;=\; \max \sum_{j \in J} c_j\, x_j
\qquad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{j \in J} a_j\, x_j \le d \quad \text{(weeks)}, \qquad x_j \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\ \ \forall j \in J

Its value function $`z(d)`$ comes from a short recurrence: with $`d`$ weeks, either leave one week unused or end with one more package. The program also tests, at each $`d`$, which slopes $`p`$ satisfy the touching-line inequality above. A price must be at least every forward slope $`(z(e) - z(d)) / (e - d)`$ for $`e > d`$, and at most every backward slope for $`e < d`$:

for d in range(0, 22):
    up = max((z[e] - z[d]) / (e - d) for e in range(d + 1, D + 1))        # a price must be at least this
    down = min([(z[d] - z[e]) / (d - e) for e in range(d)] or [math.inf])  # ... and at most this
    support = f"any p in [{up:.3f}, {down:.3f}]" if up <= down else "none"

The column LP is the LP relaxation's value, $`\tfrac{10}{7} d`$: the 7-week package has the best value per week, 10/7 ≈ 1.429, and the relaxation buys fractions of it. A price exists at $`d = 0, 7, 14, 21`$, the budgets where the integer value meets the LP's line, so the integrality gap is zero there. It is the LP's price, 1.429. At every other budget no line touches $`z`$ from above, so no single number can be "the value of one more crew-week". At $`d = 4`$, for example, the next week is worth 3 ($`z(5) - z(4)`$), so a price must be at least 3; but the week before was worth nothing ($`z(4) = z(3)`$), so a price must be at most 0. Both cannot hold.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A MILP's Dual Is a Function, Not a Number

The LP dual of lesson 2.3.1 gives each row a price $`p`$, and a plan's bound is $`p \times`$ the right side. Integer programming theory keeps the idea of a dual, a problem whose every feasible answer bounds every plan, but lets the price be any function $`F`$ of the right side instead of a straight line through zero. This is the **subadditive dual** of Jeroslow and Johnson, surveyed by Güzelsoy and Ralphs (section 3). They write it for minimization, where $`F`$ must be subadditive; for a maximization like ours the same rules hold with every inequality turned around, and $`F`$ must be **superadditive**: $`F(d) + F(e) \le F(d + e)`$ for all $`d, e`$.
For the package problem, a function $`F`$ on $`0, 1, \dots, D`$ is **dual feasible** when

and then $`F(d)`$ bounds every plan's value with $`d`$ weeks. It is an upper bound and nothing more: it does not promise that some plan reaches it, nor that every plan is worth at least that much, and it does not price the next week. The proof is three steps. A plan uses its weeks on packages and leaves $`s \ge 0`$ unused, so $`d = \sum_j a_j x_j + s`$. Apply superadditivity once per package bought and once per unused week:
F(d) \;\ge\; \sum_{j} x_j\, F(a_j) + s\,F(1) \;\ge\; \sum_{j} c_j\, x_j .

This is **weak duality**. **Strong duality** holds too: the value function $`z`$ is itself dual feasible, and $`F = z`$ gives $`F(d) = z(d)`$, the best plan exactly (Güzelsoy and Ralphs, Theorem 6, due to Jeroslow and to Wolsey). The program checks four candidate functions against the rules:

value function z         dual feasible                F(4) = 4.00 vs z = 4, F(20) = 28.00 vs z = 28
LP price 10d/7           dual feasible                F(4) = 5.71 vs z = 4, F(20) = 28.57 vs z = 28
rounded LP floor(10d/7)  dual feasible                F(4) = 5.00 vs z = 4, F(20) = 28.00 vs z = 28
price 1.3d               breaks F(3) >= 4; F(5) >= 7; F(7) >= 10 F(4) = 5.20 vs z = 4, F(20) = 26.00 vs z = 28
Read the four rows in order:

items: **The value function** is dual feasible and exact at every budget, as strong duality promises.

**The LP price** $`\tfrac{10}{7}d`$ is the linear dual function: feasible, so a valid bound, but loose (5.71 against 4 at $`d = 4`$). The LP dual is the subadditive dual restricted to straight lines, which is why its bound has a gap.

**The rounded LP price** $`\lfloor \tfrac{10}{7} d \rfloor`$ is not linear, yet it is superadditive (rounding down two numbers loses at least as much as rounding down their sum), so it is feasible. It closes the gap at $`d = 20`$ and narrows it at $`d = 4`$ (5, where the LP price gave 5.71). Functions built from rounded linear ones like this are how cutting planes (lesson 3.3.1) tighten an LP.

**The price 1.3 per week** fails every column rule: 1.3 × 7 = 9.1 is less than the 7-week package's value of 10. Its "bound" at $`d = 20`$, 26, is below a plan GridCap can actually buy (worth 28), so it bounds nothing.

blocks.text: So a MILP does have a dual, but its answer is a function of the whole right side, not a number per row, and "the value of the next unit" depends on where you stand on that function. No solver hands you that function. Computing it means knowing the best plan at every right side, which is harder than solving the MILP once. Güzelsoy and Ralphs (section 4.7) show that a finished branch-and-cut tree does contain one valid dual function, assembled from the LP duals at its leaves, but MathOpt does not expose the tree. In practice, then, a MILP is priced in two other ways, which the rest of this module teaches. Lesson 9.2.2 fixes the integers and reads LP prices that hold under that condition. Lessons 9.2.3 and 9.2.4 re-solve at many budgets and read $`V(B)`$ directly.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **A solver reports no dual values for a MILP.** MathOpt says so with `has_dual_feasible_solution() == False`, and `dual_values` raises `ValueError`; check the flag before reading prices.

**The LP relaxation has a price, but it prices a plan nobody can fund.** Its prices still bound every integer plan (weak duality), but the bound is not tight: on the small portfolio it is $115.3k above the best plan.

**A price is a line that touches the value function from above, and a step function has almost none.** The MILP's $`V(B)`$ steps; a price exists only where the integer value meets the LP's line, and there it is the LP's price.
**A MILP's dual is a function, not a number.** Any superadditive $`F`$ with $`F(0) = 0`$ that covers every column's value bounds every plan; the value function is the best such $`F`$.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: Does a MILP solve return dual values?
What does the LP relaxation's price give?
An upper bound on every integer plan, with a gap; it prices fractional projects
When does a single price support $`V`$ at $`B`$?
When $`V(B') \le V(B) + p(B' - B)`$ for every $`B'`$; for a MILP, only where the integrality gap is zero
A function $`F`$ of the right side: superadditive (max) or subadditive (min), $`F(0) = 0`$, each column's value covered
$`F(b) \ge`$ every plan's value for every dual-feasible $`F`$
The value function is dual feasible and exact

Challenges

items: In the package problem, add a 2-week package worth $25k. Predict the new LP price per week, and at which $`d`$ a price exists now.
Is $`F(d) = 4\lfloor d/3 \rfloor`$ dual feasible for the package problem? Find the first rule it breaks, or argue that it breaks none.
The finance partner says: "The LP relaxation is within 0.5% of the MILP, so its price is good enough." What does the touching-line test say about that argument at 38,380?

blocks.text: Design Note: Read the Flag, Not the Exception

A pricing report that wraps `dual_values` in `try` works, but it hides the reason. Check `has_dual_feasible_solution()` and the model's type before reading prices, and say in the report which kind of price it is: an LP's shadow price, a relaxation's price, or a fixed-integer price (lesson 9.2.2). The three answer different questions.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**no_duals.py.** Solves the selection model as a MILP and as its LP relaxation, shows the missing duals, the gap, the price's sign checked with $1k more budget, and the step that breaks concavity (*the first three sections*). *Try:* Change the budget to 38,410. Predict whether the LP relaxation still has a fractional project.

**integer_dual.py.** Computes the package problem's value function, finds where a price supports it, and checks four candidate dual functions (*the last two sections*). *Try:* Change the 7-week package's value from 10 to 9. Predict which package now sets the LP price, and where a price exists.
